Since the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in 1994 and entered into force in 1996, Countries around the world have increasingly recognized that desertification, land degradation and drought are challenges that transcend national borders and must be addressed collectively by humanity. Over this period, one of the greatest achievements of the international community has been to bring land to the center of development agenda. Today, the world recognizes that land degradation is not merely an issue of soil and vegetation. It's a complex ecosystem issue inextricably linked to food, water, livelihoods, poverty, health, migration, economy, peace and security. An important outcome. of the convention is that countries have incorporated their goal of achieving land degradation neutrality into their national policies, developed their systems for science, monitoring and reporting, and engaged not only governments but also the private sector, civil society and local communities in land restoration. Yet today, the time has come for us to ask ourselves a bold and candid question. We have spoken at length and made many declarations, but have we been able to turn our words into action? The 16th session of the Conference of the Parties held in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, marked an important step in advancing the issues of land degradation, drought resilience, land restoration, financing, science, innovation, and rangelands and pastoralists at the global policy level. Subsequently, the 23rd session of the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention held in Panama further highlights the need to strengthen implementation at the national level and to improve reporting, capacity and the science-policy interface. All previous sessions have produced meaningful outcomes, yet it's also true that the world has never lacked goals and commitments. What we need more urgently now are the resources, financing, technology, and institutional environment to turn those commitments into tangible results. Therefore, I wish to emphasize that COP17 should not be a conference where we repeat previous decisions and declarations, but rather accelerate implementation. As the Prime Minister and the Head of the Government of Mongolia, distinguished delegates, Mongolia, our vast country, is among those most severely affected by the challenges facing the world today. On this vast territory, where there are only two people for every square kilometer, 77% of our land, or in other words, eight out of every ten steps of land is affected by desertification and land degradation and is increasingly being covered by encroaching sands. Since joining the Convention, Mongolia has consistently pursued policies to combat land degradation and desertification. We have set our national target of achieving land degradation neutrality and are integrating sustainable rangeland management, the protection of forests, water and soil, and land restoration into our development policies. Climate change, drought, dzud, water scarcity and rangeland degradation are causing serious harm to the livelihoods of herder households engaged in our traditional pastoralism, as well as to food and national security, rural development, economy, and resilience of our nomadic culture. The Building Trees National Movement initiated by the President of Mongolia is a clear example of this effort. We are not simply planting trees. We are working towards long-term results in restoring ecosystems, protecting soil, water, and biodiversity, and reducing the adverse impacts of climate change. The intellectual and cultural heritage of Mongolian people is deeply rooted in our reverence and care of nature. As one of the world's last nomadic peoples, Mongolians have preserved the way of life rooted in taking only what's needed from nature. Even when hunting, we would leave a share for the wolf rather than take more than necessary. Even when picking a tree or picking a flower, we would ask nature's blessing. We have preserved this distinct way of life as a defining characteristic of our nation, living without leaving anything unnecessary behind in nature. In essence, ours is a culture that does not live to consume, but consumes only what is needed to live. Mongolians have long celebrated our mountains, rivers, and lakes in countless songs and poems, bestowed upon them official titles, and revered and worshiped them as sacred. Yet today, thousands of our once blue lakes and crystal clear rivers and streams remain only in songs, old photographs, and images. One of the most precious and unique aspects of our culture that we can showcase to the world is our millennial old knowledge and traditions associated with rangelands and nomadic pastoralism. Nomadic pastoralism is a way of life built not on confronting nature, but on living in harmony with it. By carrying forward this ancient heritage and using our rangeland wisely, we will continue our efforts to strengthen food systems, sustain the livelihoods of herder communities, conserve biodiversity and soil and water resources. The United Nations designation of 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists at the initiative Mongolia provides a historic opportunity to advance these issues at the global policy level. By linking this opportunity with COP17, Mongolia seeks to fulfill its goal of promoting a broader global understanding of rangelands. not simply as land undergoing degradation, but as vital ecosystems that require investment, generate economic value, and connect food, nature, and the livelihoods of pastoralist communities. For us, land restoration is not a matter at odds with development policies. Rather, we need to change our approach to the quality and inclusive of development. Our goal is to make environmental protection a driver of economic growth, use natural resources responsibly, and lay the foundation for long-term sustainable development based on innovation, technology, and investment. My government is implementing the Unlock Mongolia national initiative to reduce red tape for citizens and businesses, unnecessary regulations, and excessive state intervention, while promoting economic freedom, private sector growth, and free competition. As an important component of this initiative, under the Unlocking Green Development Framework, we have enacted Mongolia's first dedicated law on climate change by the State Great Hural of Mongolia, accelerated energy transition, and are ushering in a new era of environmental protection and restoration based on the participation of citizens, the private sector, and local communities. Most importantly, for a landlocked developing country such as Mongolia, the green transition is becoming a pathway to reducing our dependence on imported fuel and energy, one of the fundamental challenges constraining our economic development. To expand renewable energy from solar and wind sources, address our energy shortages, enable every household to become an energy producer, and attract interest and active participation of investors, we have reduced administrative procedures fivefold and shortened the approval process from six months to just 11 days. This year, we have begun implementing a number of renewable energy projects, and hundreds of households are already starting to become energy producers. Our journey of unlocking green development, moving from coal to solar, is well underway with strong momentum. At a time when the world witnesses fuel shortage due to a range of geopolitical factors, we are taking a number of policy and financing measures to increase the use of electric vehicles for personal use, public transport, mining and freight. As a result, people's behaviors and attitudes are changing. People are gaining more choices and the transition towards green transport is underway. This summer, in partnership with the private sector, we established Mongolia's first 60 fast charging stations for electric vehicles. This marks the beginning of our efforts to connect our vast country through a network of green stations. Drawing inspiration from our history, when a network of relay stations increased across much of the world in 13th century, I am confident that we can once again connect our country through a network of green stations. Building on our newly enacted law on climate change and the opportunities available for us to participate in carbon markets, we are developing the nomads of the sunny steppe program. Through this program, we aim to bring together within one integrated system the livelihoods of herder households, sustainable rangeland management, livestock health, product quality, market access, and export competitiveness. Our goal is to establish a system in which herders who protect and manage their rangelands responsibly earn higher incomes, herders who produce quality and high-value products receive greater returns, and local communities that restore ecosystems and support renewable energy benefit from the economic gains. We are also gradually introducing artificial intelligence, remote sensing, geographic information systems, and satellite technologies into land monitoring and natural resource management. Our goal is to establish a system that not only measures environmental challenges, but also anticipates risks and enables us to plan policies and investments based on evidence. Another important initiative under the Unlocking Green Development Framework is to establish a nationwide network of smart green schools, providing future generations with education for sustainable development in environmentally friendly settings with green infrastructure. Furthermore, building on the unique ecosystem in which Mongolia is called steppe region, we aim to create a legal and regulatory framework for developing green data centers and contribute to global innovation and technological progress. If we can achieve this, we will no longer have to choose between protecting the environment and sustaining people's livelihoods. Instead, we can create a new model of development in which the more we protect nature, the more we have increased income, and the more income increases, the stronger the incentive to protect nature, where one reinforces the other. Distinguished guests and delegates, The greatest change we expect from COP17 is a shift from words to action, from targets to implementation, and from commitments to measurable results. Therefore, Mongolia calls on this conference to make tangible progress in the following areas. First, let us address land, climate, and biodiversity not as separate issues, but as interconnected and integrated challenges. Second, let us increase investment in land restoration and bring cooperation among governments, international financial institutions, and the private sector to a new level. Third, let us make drought resilience not merely an environmental policy, but a core component of development policy. Fourth, let us place rangelands, pastoralists, and the knowledge and participation of local communities at the center of global land management policies. Fifth, let us turn science, technology, and innovation into real solutions and real investment. Sixth, let us work together to create an enabling environment for implementation that turns commitments into measurable results. To this end, we call for new partnerships with development partners, international financial institutions, the private sector, and countries to address barriers to financing, technology, capacity, and regulatory frameworks. Distinguished guests and delegates, the global community is running late to achieve the sustainable development goals by 2030. The most important outcome of our gathering here today should not simply be the adoption of decisions with modest commitments after many hours of discussion and negotiation. Rather, it should be concrete agreements that define our next steps, measurable results, and partnerships that can be implemented. For example, as part of Mongolia's preparations for COP17, the Office of the President of Mongolia established the National Green Lab, a public-private partnership platform. I call personally on all delegates and partner organizations to learn more about these projects and to support Mongolia's innovative green initiatives. As the host and president of the first of the three Rio Conventions COPs to be held this year, Mongolia is committed to working closely with the presidencies of the other two conventions to strengthen policy synergy and cooperation. Mongolia is determined to make this conference a platform for solutions. We will listen to all voices, respect different positions, and promote dialogue based on consensus that is open, transparent and inclusive. I believe that the 17th session of the Conference of the Parties beginning here amid Mongolia's vast steppes will mark a historic turning point, one at which the world recognizes that restoring land is not merely one objective of environmental protection, but a foundation for human development, livelihoods, food security, peace, and shared prosperity. Let us cherish and protect our Mother Earth, the birthplace of humanity, and create more together than we have created before, so that humanity may live in peace and endure forever. Let us restore our land, let us restore our hope, and let us build our future together.
